reasoning_traces.think:
The cognitive architecture described hinges on a dual-process model where sensation and perception are not discrete entities but interdependent cognitive functions. Sensation is defined as the immediate apprehension of simple qualities—such as pain or color—without relational context. Perception, however, integrates these sensations into meaningful representations through contextual and prior knowledge. This duality implies that while sensation may be modeled as a direct mapping from stimulus to neural response, perception requires recursive feedback mechanisms. In GSI, this translates to a hierarchical Bayesian framework where sensory data is processed through layers of belief updating, with perception acting as a higher-order inference engine. In GSE, the same structure supports dynamic state transitions, where perception acts as a control signal influencing action selection. The mutual dependence of these functions suggests a non-linear feedback loop, where each modulates the other’s efficacy. Failure modes include sensory overload (where S dominates P), perceptual hallucination (where P dominates S), and cognitive dissonance (when F_S and F_P become misaligned). These regimes define operational boundaries for both systems.
